newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritian finance minister focuses on medium term.
newsitem.headline: Mauritian finance minister focuses on medium term.

text.p: The new finance minister of Mauritius on Tuesday laid plans before parliament to speed up growth and restore economic confidence in three years.

"The elaboration and dissemination of such a policy framework aims at giving renewed dynamism to our economy and at inspiring greater confidence on the part of both local and foreign investors, and, indeed, in our population at large," Vasant Bunwaree, appointed finance minister three weeks ago, told parliament.

In his first major policy speech, he said setting medium-term targets would help remove a "wait and see" attitude prevailing in Mauritian businesses. He blamed a lack of investment for job creation failing to keep pace with those entering the labour market.
"As more and more first-time job seekers join the market, creation of jobs in traditional sectors of activity as well as in new areas will have to be accelerated," Bunwaree said.
Bunwaree seeks economic growth of 5.5 to 6.5 percent over the next three years by raising the investment rate from 24.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1996 to 30 percent by the year 2000.
"We aim at increasing the share of private investment in total investment from its present ratio of 65 percent to reach 80 percent by the end of the century," Bunwaree said.
To meet this goal, Bunwaree also aimed to raise the savings rate in the Mauritian economy to 28 percent of GDP by the year 2000 from 23.8 percent in 1996.

As an immediate measure to raise savings, Bunwaree said the government would issue 1.5 billion rupees of Mauritius Development Loan Stocks (bonds) during the first fortnight of 1997, with maturities ranging from 10 to 20 years.

"While encouraging banks to step up efforts for mobilisation of savings, the (bonds) issue will also help to contain inflationary pressures in the economy by providing long-term investment outlets," Bunwaree said.
He forecast inflation in 1996 at around 6.5 percent from 6.0 percent in 1995. Inflation is expected to fall below 5.0 percent by the century's end.
Bunwaree aimed to reduce the government's budget deficit to 2.0 percent of GDP by fiancial year 1999/2000 from 5.8 percent in 1995/96 and from a revised forecast of 4.6 percent in 1996/97.

"To reduce the fiscal deficit, measures will have to be taken both on the expenditure and revenue fronts. On the expenditure side, the objective would be to reduce the ratio of net total expenditure to GDP from the current level of 26 percent to around 23 percent by the year 1999/2000," he said.
"This will be achieved by cutting down wastage and ensuring more value for money spent in the public sector. To this end, we are accelerating reform of the parastatal sector," he added.
On the revenue side, the government aims to raise it from a present 19 percent of GDP to about 21 percent by 1999/2000 through further reforming the tax system.
